en: Having bowed his head with a purified mind to Prajāpati, the presiding lord of the Yuga consisting of five years, whose limbs are the days, seasons, half-years, and months; ||1||
I shall proclaim in due order the meritorious Jyotiṣām Ayana,
which is esteemed in the world by Brahmins for the purpose of determining the proper times for sacrifice.
For the Vedas indeed exist for the sake of sacrifice, and sacrifices are ordained according to the sequence of time;
therefore, he who knows Jyotiṣa knows this science of the prescription of time, and he knows the sacrifices. (3)
Just as the crest is to peacocks and as jewels are to serpents, so too does astrology stand at the head of the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas. //4//
Those signs beginning with Pisces that have been traversed by Jupiter,
when divided by five, the remainder is the *parigraha*.
They declare that the knowledge of time for the five-year yuga begins with the bright fortnight of Māgha and concludes with the dark fortnight of Pauṣa. ||5||

When the Moon and the Sun, together with Indra, ascend their respective paths simultaneously, then it is the first Yuga; [the month is] Māgha, the season is Tapas, the fortnight is the bright one, and the solstice is the northern.
At the beginning of Śraviṣṭhā, the sun and moon move toward the north;
however, during the latter half of Āśleṣā, the sun always moves southward in the months of Māgha and Śrāvaṇa.
The increase of the waters is one *prastha*, and their decrease occurs during the northern course;
during the southern course, these two are reversed. This change occurs by means of the six-muhūrta transition.
They say that the first, the seventh, the thirteenth beginning from the start of the transit,
and likewise the fourth and the tenth— these two pairs [are auspicious] even during the dark fortnight of the menstrual cycle.
Vasu, Tvaṣṭṛ, Bhava, Aja, Mitra, Sarpa, the two Aśvins, Jala, Dhātṛ, Ka, and the Āyana-s are the lords of the four quarters; the fifth half belongs to Ṛtu. (10)
On alternate days and months, the latter [element] follows after having placed the former first;
in the two halves of five years, they are respectively soft and [hard], being the fifteenth and the eighth.
If this day is a joint-day (parva), then the pāda [of the lunar month] consists of thirty-one parts;
one should indicate the portions by dividing them into fractional units if there is an excess.
The number twelve multiplied by two and doubled is called *gatasañjñika*;
when increased by sixty for each of two conjunctions (*parvan*), it is said to be the aggregate of the *parvas*. (13)

The Parvan-kālas are established as lasting for one, two, three, or four days; they are equal to a quarter, a half, three-quarters, or a full day, while others are measured at five days, like the moon at its equinox.
The degrees should be made into groups of eight, arising from twelve fortnights;
[the result] is diminished by eleven times [the remainder], and if it is the bright fortnight, half [is subtracted] if it belongs to the moon.
The portion increased by nine would be diminished when multiplied by seven;
in the case of an odd number, there is an insertion (āvāpa), while in the Paulastya [system], it is the other half when the sun has set.

One should know that the parvan occurs in the first half [of the month] when it is equal to the degrees of the *jāva*, and in the latter half when it exceeds them; the commencement of the lunar day (*bhādāna*) would be on the fourteenth [tithi], with the *kalās* of the *kāṣṭhās* being diminished by one.
Jau, drā, gaḥ, khe, śve, hī, ro, ṣā, ścit, mūṣakṇyaḥ, sūmādhāṇaḥ, re, mṛghāḥ, svāpojaḥ, kṛṣyaḥ, ha, jyeṣṭhā—these are the Ṛkṣas by their characteristic marks. 18.
In the place of the eighth part of the degrees (bhāṃśa), nineteen minutes (kalā) should be made;
in the place of the deficient [minutes], seventy-three should be added when a deficiency occurs.
Having multiplied the lunar day by eleven and added the degrees of the parvan, one should determine the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) of the lunar day by dividing by the total number of degrees. ||20||

Among those digits (kalās) that constitute the portions of the lunar day (tithi), one should discern through reasoning the sevenfold digit of the tithi; such are the digits that form the portions of the lunar day.
One should subtract twice the lunar day from the past portions of the cycles;
within those mandala-portions, the sun reaches its culmination according to the lunar day. (22)
The equinox (viṣuvant) is doubled, decreased by one, and multiplied by six;
half of that is a fortnight (pakṣa), and half of the fortnights is known as a lunar day (tithi). ||23||
Fifty palas of water held [in a vessel] constitute one āḍhaka; from that, a droṇa is to be measured. That [droṇa], diminished by three kuḍavas, shall be the measure for a nāḍikā. ||24||
Having multiplied the lunar days by eleven and the parvas by nine,
the pair obtained shall be the current solar asterism together with its parva in due order.
Having divided the degrees of the solar asterism by nine and doubled the remainder, one obtains the daily motion;
this added to the [daily] motion of the lunar day (tithi) gives the time in days, and its conjunction with the asterism occurs every eleven days.

The remainder of the lunar day (bha-śeṣa) is divided by three; this is the portion of the day. Having subtracted the fractional part of the fourteenth [day], if the result exceeds half a day, the subsequent portion is two; in the case of the final [day], understand it to be nine. (27)
Thirty days make a month; sixty-six months make a year; six seasons make an ayana; twelve solar months make a year; and five such years constitute a yuga. (28)
For Udayāvāsa, the day-counts would be [the base] plus five;
for Ṛṣi, it would be minus sixty-two; and for the twenty-one [remaining] cities, [it would be minus] twenty-one. (29)
The thirty-fifth century belongs to Pūṣan; the one preceding it belongs to Ayanonyṛṣi.
There are four quarters of the lunar phases, and those same units constitute the divisions of the *kāṣṭhās*. (30)
Sixty-one and seventy-two *sāvana* lunar months constitute a [lunar] year;
thirty *sāvana* days plus a half-day is a * saura* [solar] month, which is the revolution of the seasons. (31)
Agni, Prajāpati, Soma, Rudra, Uditibṛhaspati, the serpents, the ancestors, Bhaga, and Aryaman as well; ||32||
Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Indra and Agni, as well as Mitra;
Indra, Nirṛti, the Waters, and likewise the Viśvedevas. ||33||
Viṣṇu, the Vasus, Varuṇa, Ajaikapād, likewise Ahirbudhnya, Pūṣan, the two Aśvins, and Yama. ||34||

These are the deities of the lunar mansions; by means of these, in the performance of a sacrifice, the name of the sacrificer derived from the lunar mansion is traditionally recorded by those learned in the scriptures. (35)
Ugrā consists of Ārdrā, Citrā, Viśākhā, Śravaṇa, and Aśvayuj;
the cruel asterisms are Maghā, Svātī, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, and that of Yama (Bharaṇī). 36.
The solar [month] together with the full-moon day is to be known as deficient by a sixty-second part when Jupiter is present;
those two intercalary months which arise at the beginning and end of the Kṛta [yuga] occur in the middle [of that period]. 37.
Ten and twenty kalās constitute two nāḍikās of a muhūrta;
thirty of those kalās of a day (dina) shall amount to six hundred and three.
The *bhayuk* consists of seven [syllables], Soma [six], and the Sun thirteen on the days;
however, the ninefold [meter] consists of five days, and the *kāṣṭhā* consists of five syllables. ||39||

Whatever remains when [the elapsed time] from the northern solstice has been subtracted from the total, and likewise from the southern solstice, that [remainder], multiplied by two and divided by sixty-one, shall be the measure of the days [of the month]. (40)
One should know that half of the total number of day-parts at every conjunction (parvan) is the remainder of the season, having calculated it together with all [the other parts]. 41.

Thus is the summary of the means; furthermore, one should fashion a day [of practice], and having brought the mass of the knowable under cultivation, one should divide it by the mass of knowledge. 42.
Lagadha has thus declared this exposition concerning the components of months, years, muhūrtas, days, seasons, solstices, and months.

The knower who understands the threefold conduct of the Moon and the Sun attains the world of the Moon and the Sun, as well as high esteem within that world, according to those who know the Vedas. 43.
Thus ends the Yājuṣajyotiṣa.
